Today in 1986, Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda for the Famicom Disk System

Note that although most of us remember the original Zelda as a cartridge, Zelda was originally made as a launch title for the Famicom Disk System, an add-on which used floppy disks. On one hand, floppy disks were cheaper than cartridges, and didn't require batteries or passwords for saving. But although it succeeded in Japan, it had problems that convinced Nintendo not to release it abroad. Floppy Disks lacked storage space even compared to cartridge, with the Famciom's being limited to 112 kilobytes. Zelda was only 64 kilobytes, but games like Super Mario Bros 3, released only a few years later, were over 200 kilobytes. Many games were released as both cartridges and floppy disks.

When the West got Zelda over a year later, there were a few differences due to the hardware. The Japanese Disk version had slightly higher sound quality, the enemy Pols Voice could be defeated by yelling into the Famicom's second controller (which had a microphone built in), and the game's credits used the developers' real names rather than pseudonyms.
